questions.stem: Which type of investment usually holds money for a fixed term at an interest rate fixed when it is opened?
options: A parcel of shares
A term deposit
An at-call savings account
An everyday transaction account
questions.explanation: A term deposit locks the money away for an agreed term at a rate set at the start. An at-call savings account lets money be withdrawn at any time and its rate can change.

questions.stem: With simple interest, the interest each year is calculated on:
options: the original principal only
the principal plus interest earned so far
the balance left after fees each month
the interest earned in the year before
questions.explanation: Simple interest is the same percentage of the original principal every year, so I = P × r × t. Interest calculated on the principal plus earlier interest is compound interest.

questions.stem: An investment earns simple interest. A graph of its total value against time is:
options: a curve that rises and then levels off
a horizontal line at the principal
a straight line rising at a constant rate
a curve that rises more steeply over time
questions.explanation: Simple interest adds the same amount every year, so the value grows linearly and the graph is a straight line whose slope is the yearly interest. A curve that gets steeper describes compound interest.

questions.stem: In the compound interest formula A = P(1 + i)^n, what do i and n stand for?
options: The rate per compounding period and the number of periods
The annual rate and the number of years in the term
The interest earned and the number of deposits made
The inflation rate and the number of years invested
questions.explanation: The formula compounds once per period, so i is the rate for one period as a decimal and n counts the periods. For 6% p.a. compounded monthly over 3 years, i = 0.06/12 = 0.005 and n = 36.

questions.stem: The present value of an investment is:
options: the balance of the account on the day it is closed
the amount that must be invested now to reach a given future value
the interest earned over the whole term of the investment
the value of the investment after inflation has been removed
questions.explanation: Present value works backwards from a target: PV = A/(1 + i)^n is the lump sum that grows to A. The interest earned is A minus PV, not PV itself.

questions.stem: Why are interest rates annualised when investments are compared?
options: Annualising removes the effect of income tax
Annualising adjusts each rate for inflation
Different compounding periods give different yearly growth
Banks must quote every rate as a monthly rate
questions.explanation: A nominal 6% p.a. compounded monthly earns more than 6% p.a. compounded yearly. Converting each to the equivalent yearly (annualised) rate puts them on a common basis. Annualising says nothing about tax or inflation.

questions.stem: $4500 is invested at 3.6% p.a. simple interest for 4 years. How much interest is earned?
questions.explanation: I = P × r × t = 4500 × 0.036 × 4 = $648. $683.84 is compound interest, which simple interest does not use, and $6480 uses 0.36 for 3.6%.

questions.stem: A term deposit of $6000 earns $810 simple interest over 3 years. What is the annual interest rate?
questions.explanation: r = I/(P × t) = 810/(6000 × 3) = 0.045, so 4.5% p.a. 13.5% is the rate for the whole 3 years, not per year.

questions.stem: How long does it take $8000 to earn $1000 at 5% p.a. simple interest?
options: 2 years
3 years
12.5 years
2.5 years
questions.explanation: t = I/(P × r) = 1000/(8000 × 0.05) = 1000/400 = 2.5 years. Each year earns $400, so 2 years gives only $800 and 3 years gives $1200.

questions.stem: An investment earns $504 simple interest at 4.2% p.a. over 2 years. What principal was invested?
questions.explanation: P = I/(r × t) = 504/(0.042 × 2) = $6000. Dividing by 0.042 alone gives $12 000, which ignores the 2 years, and using 4.2 instead of 0.042 gives $60.

questions.stem: $7500 is invested at 4.8% p.a. compounded monthly for 5 years. What is its future value, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: i = 0.048/12 = 0.004 and n = 12 × 5 = 60, so A = 7500 × 1.004^60 = $9529.81. $9481.30 compounds yearly, and $9300 is simple interest.

questions.stem: $12 000 is invested at 6% p.a. compounded quarterly for 4 years. How much interest is earned, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: i = 0.06/4 = 0.015 and n = 16, so A = 12000 × 1.015^16 = $15 227.83 and the interest is A − P = $3227.83. $2880 is simple interest at 6% for 4 years.

questions.stem: How much must be invested now at 5% p.a. compounded annually to have $20 000 in 6 years, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: PV = A/(1 + i)^n = 20000/1.05^6 = $14 924.31. Dividing by 1 + 6 × 0.05 = 1.3 gives $15 384.62, the simple interest answer.

questions.stem: $10 000 is invested for one year at 6% p.a. How much more does it earn compounded monthly than compounded annually, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: Annually: $10 600. Monthly: 10000 × 1.005^12 = $10 616.78. The difference is $16.78: more frequent compounding earns a little more at the same nominal rate.

questions.stem: What is the annualised (effective) rate for 6% p.a. compounded monthly, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Effective rate = (1 + 0.06/12)^12 − 1 = 1.005^12 − 1 = 0.061678, or 6.17%. 6.14% is the effective rate for quarterly compounding.

questions.stem: Bank A offers 5.1% p.a. compounded annually. Bank B offers 5.0% p.a. compounded monthly. Which pays more, and why?
options: Bank A, as its annualised rate is higher at 5.10%
Neither, as both rates round to 5% p.a.
Bank B, as its annualised rate is 5.0% × 12 = 60%
Bank B, as its annualised rate is about 5.12%
questions.explanation: Bank B's annualised rate is (1 + 0.05/12)^12 − 1 = 5.116%, which is more than Bank A's 5.1%. Comparing the nominal rates alone wrongly favours Bank A.

questions.stem: A savings account pays 2.4% p.a. interest, credited yearly, and charges a $4 monthly fee. What is the net return over one year on a balance of $5000?
questions.explanation: Interest = 5000 × 0.024 = $120. Fees = 12 × 4 = $48. Net return = 120 − 48 = $72. Subtracting only one month's fee gives $116.

questions.stem: $10 000 can earn 6% p.a. simple interest or 5% p.a. compounded annually. After how many whole years is the compound option first worth more?
options: It never becomes worth more
9 years
8 years
11 years
questions.explanation: After 8 years: simple $14 800 against compound $14 774.55. After 9 years: simple $15 400 against compound $15 513.28, so compound is ahead from year 9. Compound growth always overtakes linear growth eventually.

questions.stem: What simple interest rate earns the same amount over 5 years as 4% p.a. compounded annually, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Compound growth: 1.04^5 = 1.216653, so the interest is 21.6653% of the principal over 5 years. Spread evenly as simple interest, that is 21.6653/5 = 4.33% p.a. 21.67% is the total over all 5 years.

questions.stem: $5000 is invested at 4.5% p.a. compounded annually. Using technology, after how many whole years does it first exceed $7000?
options: 8 years
7 years
9 years
6 years
questions.explanation: 5000 × 1.045^7 = $6804.31, still below $7000, while 5000 × 1.045^8 = $7110.50. So 8 whole years are needed. Seven years falls just short.

questions.stem: Using technology, what annual compound rate grows $6000 to $8000 in 6 years, to two decimal places?
questions.explanation: Solve 6000(1 + r)^6 = 8000, so (1 + r)^6 = 4/3 and r = 0.049115, about 4.91%. 5.56% is the simple interest rate, which ignores compounding.

questions.stem: What is brokerage?
options: The market price of one share on the exchange
The fee a broker charges to buy or sell shares
The part of a company's profit paid to shareholders
The tax charged on the profit from selling shares
questions.explanation: Brokerage is the broker's fee for each trade, charged as a percentage of the trade value or as a flat fee, with GST added. A share of profit paid to shareholders is a dividend.

questions.stem: Compared with a term deposit, what is the main extra risk of investing in shares?
options: Shares must be held for a fixed term before they can be sold
Share dividends are fixed in advance and cannot rise
Shares pay no income until the company is wound up
The share price can fall, so the money invested is not guaranteed
questions.explanation: Share prices rise and fall with the market, so an investor can lose part of the capital. Shares can be sold at any time on the market, and dividends vary with company profits.

questions.stem: Ella buys 800 shares at $4.25 each. Brokerage is 1.2% of the trade value, plus GST. What is the total cost?
questions.explanation: Trade value = 800 × 4.25 = $3400. Brokerage with GST = 3400 × 0.012 × 1.1 = $44.88. Total = $3444.88. $3440.80 leaves out the GST on the brokerage.

questions.stem: Ella later sells her 800 shares at $5.10 each, paying brokerage of 1.2% plus GST. How much does she receive?
questions.explanation: Sale value = 800 × 5.10 = $4080. Brokerage with GST = 4080 × 0.0132 = $53.86, which is subtracted when selling: $4026.14. Adding the brokerage, as when buying, gives $4133.86.

questions.stem: Tom buys 1100 shares at $2.40 each and pays a flat brokerage fee of $30 plus GST, and will pay the same fee to sell. Using BE = b + 2.2f/n, what is his break-even price per share?
questions.explanation: BE = 2.40 + 2.2 × 30/1100 = 2.40 + 66/1100 = 2.40 + 0.06 = $2.46. Using 30 × 1.1 once gives $2.43, which covers only the buying fee.

questions.stem: Shares are bought at $5 each with brokerage of 1.5% plus GST on both buying and selling. Using BE = b(1 + 1.1r)/(1 − 1.1r), what is the break-even price, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: 1.1r = 1.1 × 0.015 = 0.0165, so BE = 5 × 1.0165/0.9835 = 5.1678, or $5.17. $5.15 leaves out the GST, and $5.08 covers only the buying cost.

questions.stem: A shareholder owns 2500 shares and the company pays a dividend of 18 cents per share. What is the dividend income?
questions.explanation: Dividend = 2500 × 0.18 = $450. Using 18 dollars or 1.8 cents per share moves the decimal point.

questions.stem: A share is priced at $12.50 and pays an annual dividend of 55 cents. What is the dividend as a percentage of the share price?
questions.explanation: Percentage dividend = 0.55/12.50 × 100 = 4.4%. 0.044% forgets to multiply the decimal 0.044 by 100, and 22.7% divides the price by the dividend instead.

questions.stem: Ella's 800 shares cost $3444.88 including brokerage. She received dividends of $96 and sold them for $4026.14 after brokerage. What is her percentage return, to one decimal place?
questions.explanation: Return = sale proceeds + dividends − cost = $4026.14 + $96 − $3444.88 = $677.26, which is 19.7% of the $3444.88 invested. 16.9% leaves out the dividends.

questions.stem: A $1200 item rises in price with inflation of 2.5% p.a. What will it cost in 4 years, to the nearest cent?
questions.explanation: Inflation compounds like interest: 1200 × 1.025^4 = $1324.58. $1320 adds 2.5% of $1200 each year, a simple interest model.

questions.stem: Sam earns $640 interest in a year and pays tax at 30 cents in the dollar on it. How much interest does he keep?
questions.explanation: Tax = 0.30 × 640 = $192, so he keeps 640 − 192 = $448. $192 is the tax paid, not the interest kept.

questions.stem: An investment earns 4.5% p.a. Interest is taxed at 30% and inflation is 3.2% p.a. Has the investment made real growth?
options: Yes: the after-tax return of 3.15% is above zero
No: the 30% tax is larger than the 4.5% return
No: the after-tax return of 3.15% is below inflation
Yes: the 4.5% return is above the 3.2% inflation
questions.explanation: After tax the return is 4.5% × 0.7 = 3.15% p.a., which is less than 3.2% inflation, so the investment's buying power is falling slightly. Comparing the 4.5% before tax with inflation ignores the tax.

questions.stem: $10 000 grows to $11 236 in 2 years. Inflation is 3% p.a. By how much does the investment beat what was needed just to keep pace with inflation?
questions.explanation: Keeping pace with inflation needs 10000 × 1.03^2 = $10 609. The investment is worth 11236 − 10609 = $627 more. $636 subtracts simple inflation of 2 × 3%.

questions.stem: Why do many people use credit to buy items rather than saving for them first?
options: Lenders pay interest to people who borrow from them
They can have the item now and pay for it over time
Credit always costs less than paying cash later
Interest is never charged on credit purchases
questions.explanation: Credit gives immediate use of the item, but interest and fees usually make the total cost higher than paying cash. That extra cost is the price of having it sooner.

questions.stem: A credit card charges 18.25% p.a. simple interest calculated daily. How much interest is charged on an unpaid balance of $1460 for 30 days?
questions.explanation: Daily rate = 0.1825/365 = 0.0005. Interest = 1460 × 0.0005 × 30 = $21.90. $266.45 is a full year's interest.

questions.stem: An $8000 personal loan has an establishment fee of $250 and repayments of $256.26 a month for 3 years. What is the total cost of the loan beyond the amount borrowed?
questions.explanation: Total paid = 36 × $256.26 + $250 = $9475.36. Cost of borrowing = $9475.36 − $8000 = $1475.36. Leaving out the fee gives $1225.36.

questions.stem: A $2400 television is bought on a store card with 12 months interest free and a $5 monthly account fee. If it is paid off within the 12 months, what is the total cost?
questions.explanation: No interest is charged, but the fee applies every month: 2400 + 12 × 5 = $2460. Interest free does not mean fee free, so $2400 understates the cost.

questions.stem: A $2000 laptop rises in price by 4% p.a. Kai could save for 2 years and then buy it, or borrow now and pay $260 interest. Which costs less, and by how much?
options: Saving, by $96.80
Borrowing, by $96.80
Saving, by $260
Borrowing, by $163.20
questions.explanation: After 2 years the laptop costs 2000 × 1.04^2 = $2163.20. Borrowing costs 2000 + 260 = $2260. Saving is cheaper by $96.80, but Kai waits 2 years for the laptop.

questions.stem: A line of credit is:
options: a loan of a fixed amount repaid in equal instalments
a savings account that pays a bonus rate of interest
a share purchase made on behalf of the investor
an approved limit that can be borrowed against as needed
questions.explanation: A line of credit lets the borrower draw funds up to an agreed limit and pay interest only on what is used. A fixed amount repaid in equal instalments describes a personal loan.
